evals.name: write-canvas-ta-integrity
evals.prompt: I'm building a Canvas module for first-time grad TAs on handling suspected academic misconduct. The module text is in evals/files/ta-academic-integrity-module.md. Can you write 6 knowledge-check questions for the end of the module that I can import into Canvas? It's a formative check, not graded.
evals.expected_output: Six scenario-based one-best-answer items grounded in the module, 4 options each, explanatory feedback on every option, no NOTA/AOTA/negative lead-ins, a Canvas-importable QTI package, no invented policy, and delivery advice suited to a formative check.
expectations: Exactly 6 questions are produced
Every question has exactly one correct option and 4 options (or states a reason for a different count)
Every option of every question, including the correct one, has feedback explaining why it is or isn't the best answer (not just 'Correct'/'Incorrect')
At least 5 of the 6 questions present a realistic situation the TA must respond to or judge, rather than asking for a definition or a fact restated from the text
No question uses 'none of the above', 'all of the above', or a negative lead-in (EXCEPT / NOT / LEAST)
A file importable into Canvas is produced (a QTI .zip package) that contains all 6 questions with their answer keys
The questions and feedback introduce no institutional policy specifics that are absent from the module (e.g. new deadlines, penalties, offices, or procedures)
The response gives Canvas delivery advice suited to a formative check (e.g. feedback display, single attempt with feedback rather than try-until-correct)
No question's correct answer is the longest of its options (by word count)
Correct answers are spread across positions: no single letter is the key for more than 3 of the 6 questions
No correct answer reuses a distinctive phrase of 5 or more consecutive words from the module text
Every distractor is a plausible, distinct choice: none is a near-duplicate of another option or obviously absurd

evals.name: review-stats-quiz
evals.prompt: A colleague drafted this week-5 quiz for our intro stats course: evals/files/stats-quiz-draft.md. Can you review it, tell me what's wrong, and give me fixed versions? It counts for 2% of the final grade.
evals.expected_output: Catches the Q3 miskey first, identifies the planted flaws (negative lead-in, NOTA and long key, combination/AOTA format, overlapping numeric options, open lead-ins, vague/absolute terms), leaves Q7 essentially intact, and supplies revised items with per-option feedback.
expectations: Identifies that Q3 is miskeyed: the keyed causal conclusion (a) is wrong and the association option (b) is correct
Presents the Q3 miskey as the most serious problem (ahead of wording or format issues)
Flags Q1's negative lead-in (NOT)
Flags Q2's 'none of the above' option and/or its over-long, over-detailed keyed answer
Flags Q4's combination / 'all of the above' format and rewrites it as a single-best-answer item
Flags Q6's overlapping numeric options (68% also falls inside '50% to 70%' and 'more than 60%')
Recognises Q7 as well constructed and keeps it, or changes it only minimally
Provides revised versions of the flawed questions, each with feedback for every option
The response opens with a short, severity-ordered summary (e.g. must fix / should fix) in plain language, with no internal flaw codes in that summary
The revised questions introduce no new flaws (no key that is the longest option, no open or negative lead-in, no distractor that could reasonably be argued correct)

evals.name: analyze-canvas-results
evals.prompt: We ran a 12-question multiple-choice quiz in Canvas last term with 140 students. I exported the responses (evals/files/quiz-responses.csv) and the answer key (evals/files/quiz-key.csv). Which questions should I fix or drop before I reuse it this term?
evals.expected_output: Flags Q4 as a likely miskey, Q11 as possibly having two defensible answers, Q7's unused distractor, and Q9 as too easy; leaves healthy items alone; reports reliability; recommends expert review rather than automatic deletion.
expectations: Identifies Q4 as likely miskeyed (strong students chose a different option; negative discrimination)
Identifies Q11 as possibly having two defensible answers (strong students split between the key D and option B)
Identifies that Q7 has a distractor (A) that almost no one chooses
Identifies Q9 as too easy to be informative
Does not recommend fixing or dropping well-performing items such as Q1, Q5, or Q12
Reports a test-level reliability estimate (e.g. KR-20 or Cronbach's alpha)
Frames the flagged items as needing content review before deciding (e.g. check the Q4 key against the question) rather than deleting them automatically
Reports what rekeying Q4 would do to last term's scores in both directions (how many students gain and how many lose a point)
Treats Q11 as a possible two-answer item to check (e.g. accept both, or revise), not as a simple miskey
Reports test reliability of about .70 (between .68 and .72) under the original key
evals.ground_truth: Generated by a seeded simulation: Q4 keyed C but the defensible answer is D; Q7 distractor A chosen by <1%; Q9 near-universal correct; Q11 strong students split between key D and B; other items healthy.
